title: Install and monitor a total quality management system for perishable produce exportation

lessons.title: Legislation, market best practice and preparation
lessons.html:
How legislation shapes a TQMS

A total quality management system (TQMS) in the export environment is built on a legal foundation. The Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 sets minimum quality, packing, marking and inspection requirements; the PPECB Act 9 of 1983 sets cold chain controls; Act 36 of 1947 governs the use of agricultural remedies; the OHS Act 85 of 1993 governs worker safety; and phytosanitary protocols of each market set pest controls. A TQMS turns these legal requirements into procedures, responsibilities and records so that compliance is the normal way of working, not a last-minute effort before inspection.

Best practices required by export markets

  • Farm level: GLOBALG.A.P. or equivalent good agricultural practice certification.
  • Packhouse level: food safety certification recognised by the buyer, often based on HACCP principles.
  • Social and ethical: audits such as SIZA covering labour conditions.
  • Environmental: water, energy, waste and biodiversity practices.
  • Retailer codes: specific requirements of each supermarket group, often stricter than law.

Integrating these into one TQMS avoids running several separate paper systems. One set of procedures and records can serve the legal inspection, the certification audit and the retailer audit.

Preparing to establish a TQMS

  1. Management commitment: owners and managers must provide time, money and leadership. Without this, the system becomes paperwork that nobody follows.
  2. Gap analysis: compare current practices against all legal and market requirements and list what is missing.
  3. Quality policy and objectives: a short statement of commitment and measurable targets, for example reduce inspection failures to below a set percentage, or zero residue exceedances.
  4. Appoint a responsible person: a quality manager or coordinator with authority.
  5. Resources: budget for training, equipment such as calibrated instruments, and possibly consultants.
  6. Communication: explain to all staff why the system is being introduced and how it will affect them.

lessons.title: Designing and implementing the system
lessons.html:
Designing to fit the organisation

A TQMS for a 20-hectare family farm with a small packshed looks very different from one for a multi-site packhouse group, but the same building blocks apply. Design the system around how the business actually works.

  • Map the processes: draw the flow from orchard to dispatch: harvest, receiving, drenching, grading, packing, palletising, cooling, storage, inspection and loading.
  • Identify risks and controls at each step: quality, food safety, phytosanitary, cold chain and safety. Use HACCP principles to identify critical control points.
  • Define responsibilities: an organogram showing who is responsible for each control, and who deputises.
  • Document structure: a quality manual or policy, procedures for each process, work instructions at the workstation, and record forms.
  • Keep it practical: short, clear procedures in the languages staff use, with pictures where helpful.

Implementing the processes

  1. Train each person on the procedures for their role and record training.
  2. Introduce records such as receiving logs, drench concentration checks, QC sample sheets, cold store temperatures and cleaning checklists.
  3. Set up specifications per market and client at the grading and packing tables.
  4. Calibrate instruments such as thermometers, penetrometers, refractometers and scales and record calibration.
  5. Establish traceability from bin to pallet to container.
  6. Introduce non-conformance handling: how to tag, isolate and decide on product that fails.
  7. Run a trial period, gather feedback and adjust procedures before full certification audits.

Example: a packhouse introduces hourly drench concentration checks. In the first week, records show long gaps on night shift. The quality manager finds that the night shift had not been trained, arranges training and adds the check to the supervisor's shift handover list.

lessons.title: Monitoring, managing and auditing the TQMS
lessons.html:
Monitoring and managing

Once running, the system must be monitored with measurable indicators. Useful indicators include:

  • PPECB inspection pass rate and reasons for failure;
  • market claims and arrival quality reports;
  • packout percentage per class;
  • residue test results;
  • cold chain compliance: time to cool, temperature deviations;
  • number and closure rate of non-conformances;
  • training completed against plan.

Review these weekly during the season. Display key results to staff so everyone sees progress. When an indicator moves the wrong way, investigate the root cause and take corrective action rather than only fixing the symptom.

Auditing to validate the process

Audits check that the system is working as designed and is effective.

  • Internal audits: planned audits by trained staff who do not audit their own work, using checklists based on procedures and standards. Cover every area at least once per season.
  • External audits: certification bodies and client audits.
  • Audit process: plan, gather evidence by observing work, interviewing staff and checking records, compare with requirements, report findings, and agree corrective actions with deadlines.
  • Follow-up: verify that corrective actions were completed and effective.

Validation and management review

Validation confirms that key controls actually achieve their purpose, for example that the cooling regime brings pulp temperature down in the required time, or that the drench controls decay. Use data from trials, research guidelines and market results.

At least once a year, top management reviews audit findings, indicators, claims, changes in legislation and market requirements, and resources. It decides on improvements and updates the quality objectives for the next season. This closes the Plan-Do-Check-Act loop.

Key points

  • A TQMS turns legal and market requirements into daily procedures and records.
  • Start with management commitment and a gap analysis.
  • Design the system around the real process flow and responsibilities.
  • Monitor indicators such as pass rates, claims and temperature deviations.
  • Internal audits, validation and management review keep the system effective.
